design_detail: Cross-sectional analysis of one year of a coroner-fed register (the authors call it a retrospective cohort study): accidental drug-related deaths reported by coroners in England and Wales to the National Programme of Substance Abuse Deaths (NP-SAD) in 2000. NP-SAD holds deaths in which a psychoactive substance was directly implicated, or in which the person had a history of drug dependence or misuse; coroners report voluntarily, supplying demographics, prescribed medication, place and circumstances of death, substances found post mortem, the coroner's verdict and the cause of death as on the death certificate, with a description of the circumstances. Deaths with a suicide verdict, an open verdict where suicidal or homicidal intent was clear, no verdict, or too little information for a causal judgement were excluded. Two researchers independently assigned each remaining death to one of six categories of cause (direct overdose, traumatic accident, toxicity with a non-drug-related medical condition, toxicity with a drug-related medical condition, acute infection, acute non-traumatic physical event) using, in order, the certificate's cause of death, the coroner's verdict, the drugs implicated, the drugs found post mortem and the coroner's report; a medical consultant specialising in addiction confirmed the categories. Agreement was measured with phi; categories were described by sex, age, employment, living arrangement, place of death and recorded history of drug misuse with 'prevalence ratios', and drugs implicated in the cause of death and found post mortem were tabulated by category. No comparison with official statistics or ICD codes.
can_establish: How the 1,037 accidental deaths that coroners in England and Wales reported to NP-SAD in 2000 divided, on these researchers' reading of the coroners' returns, between direct drug toxicity and other mechanisms (aspiration and other acute events, toxicity with a medical condition, injuries, infections), and which drugs coroners named as implicated in, or reported as found after, the deaths in each category.
cannot_establish: How many deaths official statistics counted wrongly as drug poisoning, or missed (no comparison with ONS records or ICD codes was made); any risk by sex, age, employment, living arrangement or drug (no population denominators: the 'prevalence ratios' compare numbers of deaths); whether a drug not reported was absent or untested (negative results were not recorded); or how complete NP-SAD was (coroners reported voluntarily and coverage is not stated).

sample.recruitment: Register: accidental drug-related deaths reported by coroners in England and Wales to NP-SAD, St George's Hospital Medical School, in 2000; coroners reported voluntarily (p. 68, section 2.1; p. 73).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: A drug-related fatality was defined, after Quaglio et al. (2001) and Van Haastrecht et al. (1994), as accidental overdose in cases of recent drug use under circumstances that did not suggest other causes of death; deaths were excluded as intentional or not known for a suicide verdict, an open verdict with clear suicidal or homicidal intent, no verdict, or information insufficient for a causal judgement (p. 68, section 2.2). The number of records screened and excluded is not reported.
sample.demographics: 828 men (79.8%) and 209 women; 84.3% under 45; mean age 37.7 years; 61.5% unemployed; a history of drug misuse or dependence recorded for 755 (72.8%), not for 194, unknown for 88; died at their home address 615, in hospital 305, elsewhere 117 (p. 69, section 3.3; Table 1, p. 70).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Missing values are not acknowledged: occupation is given for 1,008, living arrangement for 970 and age group for 1,035 of the 1,037 deaths (editors' sums from Table 1).
sample.selection_effects: A voluntary, coroner-fed register whose coverage is not stated; accidental deaths only; the categories are the researchers' reading of coroners' returns, which differ in detail. The Introduction notes that counts differ by source (605 coroners' verdicts of death from drug misuse and 1,296 NP-SAD drug-related deaths in 2000; 2,943 ONS drug-poisoning deaths in 1999). All authors worked for NP-SAD.

exposure.measurement: How a death entered the count, and who decided: the coroner reported it to NP-SAD with the verdict and the certified cause of death; NP-SAD's inclusion rule is stated above; the two researchers (LW and SC) independently identified accidental cases and assigned the category, and a medical consultant specialising in addiction (FS) confirmed them (pp. 68–69). Drugs 'implicated' are those named in the cause of death; drugs 'found post mortem' are as reported by coroners (pp. 71–72). What was tested: no toxicology panel, specimen or share of deaths tested is reported; NP-SAD records positive findings only, so whether a substance not reported was absent or not tested is unknown, and there was no standardized toxicological testing or reporting at inquest (p. 73). Alcohol is recorded only when present or implicated together with other drugs (p. 73).
exposure.polysubstance: Central to the tables: each drug is counted wherever it was implicated or found, alone or in combination, so rows overlap; alcohol appears only with other drugs. Sole-drug figures are given only in the text (e.g., methadone the sole drug implicated in 4% of direct overdoses) and cannot be checked against a table.

comparison.controls: No external comparison. Deaths are compared across the six categories; each 'prevalence ratio' divides the percentage of a category's deaths in one subgroup (e.g., women) by the percentage in a reference subgroup (e.g., men) within the same category.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (counts of deaths). The population of people who use drugs from which the deaths arose, by sex, age or employment, is unknown, so no risk can be computed.

outcomes.instruments: Category of cause of death (six categories defined on pp. 68–69); agreement between the two researchers (phi); Table 1 demographics by category with prevalence ratios (p. 70); Table 2 drugs implicated by category (p. 71); Table 3 drugs found post mortem by category (p. 72).
outcomes.validity_norms: The categories are the authors' own and not validated against any reference; agreement phi 0.77 overall and 0.64 for acute infection.
outcomes.operationalization: Direct overdose: death directly related to an episode of toxicity, including its physiological consequences (respiratory depression, pneumonia, anoxia, renal failure, multiple organ failure). Traumatic accident: injury from behaviour related to intoxication (e.g., road traffic accident, drowning, electrocution). Non-drug-related and drug-related medical condition: toxicity superimposed on a pre-existing condition mentioned as a contributing cause (e.g., asthma, epilepsy, heart disease; or hepatitis B or C, endocarditis, cirrhosis). Acute infection related to an episode of drug use (e.g., septicaemia, acute endocarditis, necrotising fasciitis). Acute physical event: e.g., aspiration of gastric contents, postural asphyxia or hypothermia, where intoxication likely impaired self-protection.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. About 50 prevalence ratios in Table 1 are flagged only by whether their 95% CI lies above or below 1; no intervals are printed.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; the researchers classified deaths from the full coroners' returns.

analysis.effect_sizes: Categories: direct overdose 802 (77%); acute physical event 74 (7%); drug-related medical condition 72 (7%); non-drug-related medical condition 40 (4%); traumatic accident 31 (3%); acute infection 18 (2%). Agreement (phi): 0.77 overall; direct overdose 0.85; traumatic accident 0.92; acute event 0.88; medical conditions 0.72; acute infection 0.64 (agreement on 11 of 18). Heroin/morphine implicated in 424 (53%) and found in 488 (60.8%) of direct overdoses; implicated in 11 of 18 acute infections (61%), 33 of 72 drug-related medical conditions (46%), 42 of 74 acute physical events (57%) and 9 of 31 traumatic accidents (29%). Alcohol implicated in 232 (29%) and found in 316 (39.4%) of direct overdoses; implicated in 15 (48%) and found in 17 (54.8%) traumatic accidents. Cocaine implicated in 35 (4%) and found in 74 (9.2%) direct overdoses; implicated in 8 (26%) traumatic accidents. Editors' sums across all categories, implicated against found: heroin/morphine 528 against 601; alcohol 300 against 397; hypnotics and sedatives 129 against 291; cocaine 56 against 105; amphetamines 19 against 41. Prevalence ratios are ratios of within-category percentages (e.g., women 20.3% and men 79.9% of direct overdoses give 0.3; editors' check), so they describe the make-up of each category, not risk.
analysis.selective_reporting: Sole-drug figures appear only in the text; the numbers screened and excluded are not given; confidence intervals for the prevalence ratios are not printed; no breakdown of drug by medical condition supports the statements on infections and on amphetamines and heart disease.
analysis.power: Not applicable. Several ratios rest on very small numbers, e.g., the drug-related medical condition ratio of 30.0 for ages 25–34 against 15–24 compares 30 deaths with 1 (editors' calculation from Table 1).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 1,037 accidental deaths that coroners in England and Wales reported to NP-SAD in 2000, the researchers placed 802 (77%) in direct overdose, the default category when nothing suggested otherwise (an upper limit), and 235 (23%) in five other categories: 74 acute physical events (mostly aspiration of gastric contents), 72 toxicity with a drug-related medical condition, 40 toxicity with another medical condition, 31 traumatic accidents and 18 acute infections. Drugs named as implicated in the deaths were fewer than those reported as found post mortem (e.g., cocaine implicated in 56 deaths and found in 105, editors' sums).
interpretation_gap.claimed: (1) The abstract presents the 23% as the "'masked' manner of death in cases typically recorded as overdose" (p. 67), but no comparison with official statistics, ICD codes or how these deaths were certified was made, and 112 of the 235 are by the authors' own definitions drug toxicity superimposed on a medical condition. (2) The abstract and Results speak of higher or lower risk by sex, age, employment, living arrangement and history of drug misuse, but the prevalence ratios compare numbers of deaths within each category, with no population denominators; the Results (25–34-year-olds at highest risk in all categories) and the Discussion (risk decreasing from age 25 for overdose, trauma, acute events and infections) also read the same table in opposite ways (pp. 69, 72). (3) The abstract's statements that heroin/morphine use carries further risks from acute infection and from HIV, HBV or HCV, and that amphetamine use was most associated with cardiovascular death, rest on counts of drugs implicated within small categories (11 of 18 acute infections; amphetamines in 6 of 40 non-drug-related medical-condition deaths) without any cross-tabulation of drug by condition. (4) The Discussion reads methadone's 13% share of direct overdoses as support for reduced mortality in treatment, which a share of deaths cannot show. (5) The Discussion's suggestions (recovery-position education, take-home naloxone, fear of prosecution delaying first aid) are not tested by these data. (6) The design is called a retrospective cohort study; it is a cross-sectional series of deaths.

timeline.event: Brettle et al. (as cited, p. 68): among pre-AIDS deaths of HIV-positive people who injected drugs, 45% were direct accidental overdoses and 24% of drug-related deaths were associated with an underlying drug-related medical condition.

Counts by source quoted in the Introduction (p. 67): coroners' verdicts of death from drug misuse rose from 573 to 605 in 2000 (Allen, 2001); NP-SAD recorded 1,296 drug-related deaths in 2000; ONS reported 2,943 deaths in England and Wales in 1999 with drug poisoning as the underlying cause (ONS, 2001).
Gossop et al. (as cited, p. 73): the cause of death on death certificates is often imprecise or ill-founded, and routine recording of all substances found by toxicology could improve accuracy.

Beynon et al. (card sc_beynon_2007): of 70 deaths that np-SAD reported as drug-related for Liverpool (2004 to mid-2005), 25 were not deaths from drug toxicity (that card's arithmetic); np-SAD's definition is wider than the UK Drug Strategy definition used for national statistics.

Chen et al. compared ONS data with data of the National Programme on Substance Use Mortality (NPSUM); by its title, opioid-related deaths in England and Wales have been systematically underestimated. Listed for this page; not read for this card.

replication.where_it_stands: That a substantial share of deaths in the coroner-fed register were not direct toxicity deaths is consistent with the Liverpool review of np-SAD deaths (card sc_beynon_2007), which found about a third were not drug-toxicity deaths. Neither study compared its categories with how the same deaths were counted in ONS statistics, so the size of any overcount in official drug-poisoning figures remains unmeasured by these papers. The comparison of ONS and NPSUM counts (Chen et al., 2025) addresses the opposite direction and has not been read here.

funding.funder: Not reported: the article has no funding statement.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the article has no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: All six authors were at the National Programme of Substance Abuse Deaths, St George's Hospital Medical School, London, the programme whose register is analysed (p. 67); the corresponding author's address is the University of Salford. The Discussion argues for wider coroner reporting to NP-SAD (p. 73). Recorded as a flag for closer reading.

what_would_settle_it: Linking the same coroner-reported deaths to their ONS mortality records (underlying cause and all codes) and to complete toxicology results, including negative ones, with two blinded pathologists classifying the mechanism of death, would show how many deaths counted as drug poisoning in official statistics had another mechanism and how many drug-related deaths official statistics missed; statements about risk would also need population denominators.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: NP-SAD was fed voluntarily by coroners; its coverage of drug-related deaths in England and Wales in 2000 is not stated.
All accidental cases were meant to be included, but the number of records screened and excluded under the four exclusion rules is not reported.
1,037 deaths overall; the non-overdose categories are small (18 to 74), so their breakdowns are imprecise.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Table 1 describes the deaths in each category by sex, age, employment, living arrangement, place of death and recorded history of drug misuse.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: All deaths are categorised, but missing values for occupation (29), living arrangement (67) and age (2) are not acknowledged.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: The categories have written definitions, but they overlap (pneumonia under direct overdose, aspiration pneumonia under acute events), the stated case definition conflicts with including injury and medical-condition deaths, and no external reference was used.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Two independent raters and a confirming consultant, phi 0.77 overall and 0.64 for acute infection; how disagreements were resolved is not described, and coroners' returns vary in detail and lack negative toxicology.

Ratios of within-category percentages are presented as risks, without population denominators, printed intervals or correction; several ratios and percentages in Tables 1 and 2 do not match their own counts.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Coroners reported voluntarily; the proportion of coroners or eligible deaths reported is not given.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI-prevalence fits a description of deaths in a register by category (round brief, certificate and register studies). The frame's completeness and the exclusions are not reported, the categories are the researchers' unvalidated reading with moderate agreement, and the comparative statistics are inappropriate for the risk statements made from them; several table values are internally inconsistent. Citable for: among 1,037 accidental deaths that coroners in England and Wales reported to NP-SAD in 2000, the researchers judged 77% direct overdoses and 23% other mechanisms (aspiration and other acute events, toxicity with medical conditions, injuries, infections); drugs reported as found after death outnumbered those named as implicated (e.g., cocaine 105 against 56); alcohol was found in nearly 40% of these deaths. Not citable for: overcounting in official statistics, any risk by sex, age, employment or drug, or associations of particular drugs with particular conditions.

key_findings.finding: Of 1,037 accidental drug-related deaths reported by coroners in England and Wales to NP-SAD in 2000, the researchers classed 802 (77%) as direct acute overdose; the remaining 23% were 31 traumatic accidents (3%), 40 toxicity with a non-drug-related medical condition (4%), 72 toxicity with a drug-related medical condition (7%), 18 acute infections (2%) and 74 acute non-traumatic physical events (7%).
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Causes of death, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (column headings)
key_findings.note: The five non-overdose categories total 235 deaths (editors' calculation). Direct overdose was the default category when nothing suggested otherwise (p. 68), so 77% is an upper limit (reporting issue 1).

key_findings.finding: Conditions named by coroners within categories: aspiration of gastric contents in 42 cases of direct aspiration asphyxia and 22 of aspiration pneumonia, 6 postural asphyxia, 1 hypothermia; road traffic accidents in 11 traumatic deaths, others from drowning, falls, electrocution and railway accidents; across the two medical-condition categories, 21 pre-existing cardiac conditions, 6 cardiac arrests indirectly associated with substance misuse, 13 pneumonia or bronchopneumonia, 2 epilepsy, 5 renal disease, 6 asthma, 16 chronic infections or illnesses (including HIV), and liver disease in 39 (hepatitis B and C, cirrhosis, fatty liver); acute infections were specified in 20 cases (necrotising fasciitis, septicaemia, endocarditis).
key_findings.note: 20 cases with acute infection specified against 18 deaths in the acute infection category; the difference is not explained. The 13 pneumonia cases are printed in words (Thirteen).

key_findings.finding: Agreement between the two researchers who independently identified and categorised the deaths (phi): 0.77 overall; 0.85 direct acute overdose; 0.92 traumatic accident; 0.88 acute event; 0.72 drug-related and non-drug-related medical conditions; 0.64 acute infection, where they agreed on 11 of 18 cases. A medical consultant specialising in addiction confirmed the categories.
key_findings.locator: 2.3 Case categorisation, last paragraph; 3.1 Concordance ratings

key_findings.finding: Who and what decided the category: a hierarchy of evidence, in order, of the cause of death on the death certificate, the coroner's verdict, the drugs implicated, the drugs found post mortem and additional information in the coroner's report. Direct overdose included deaths from the physiological consequences of toxicity (respiratory depression, pneumonia, anoxia, renal failure, multiple organ failure); the two medical-condition categories were toxicity superimposed on a pre-existing condition mentioned as a contributing cause.

Case definition: a drug-related fatality was accidental overdose in cases of recent drug use under circumstances not suggesting other causes; deaths were excluded for a suicide verdict, an open verdict with clear suicidal or homicidal intent, no verdict, or too little information for a causal judgement. NP-SAD includes deaths with a psychoactive substance directly implicated, or of people with a history of drug dependence or misuse; coroners supply circumstances, substances found post mortem, the verdict and the certified cause of death.
The deaths were mostly of men (79.8%), people under 45 (84.3%), unemployed people (61.5%) and people with a recorded history of drug misuse or dependence (72.8%); mean age 37.7 years.
key_findings.locator: 3.3 Causes of death and demographic characteristics, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Prevalence ratios reported as differences in risk: women against men, traumatic accident 0.1, acute physical event 0.2, drug-related medical condition 0.2, non-drug-related medical condition 0.4, acute infection 0.5; ages 25–34 against 15–24, drug-related medical condition 30.0, acute infection 10.0, direct overdose 2.3; over 45 against 15–24, traumatic accident 0.1.
key_findings.locator: 3.3 Causes of death and demographic characteristics, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1
key_findings.note: Each ratio divides two percentages from the same category column of Table 1 (e.g., women 20.3% and men 79.9% of direct overdoses give 0.3); they describe the make-up of each category's deaths, not risk (editors' check).

key_findings.finding: Heroin/morphine was implicated in 424 (53%) direct overdoses and found post mortem in 488 (60.8%); it was the drug most often implicated in acute infections (11, 61%), drug-related medical conditions (33, 46%) and acute physical events (42, 57%), and was implicated in 9 (29%) traumatic accidents.
key_findings.locator: 3.4 Substances implicated in death and cause of death, 2nd paragraph; Table 2; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Alcohol, recorded only when present or implicated with other drugs, was implicated in 300 deaths across all categories: 232 (29%) direct overdoses and 15 (48%) traumatic accidents; it was found post mortem in 316 (39.4%) direct overdoses and 17 (54.8%) traumatic accidents, and in nearly 40% of all deaths.

Cocaine was implicated in 35 (4%) direct overdoses, 2% as the sole drug, and found post mortem in 74 (9.2%); it was implicated in 8 (26%) traumatic accidents, once as the sole drug. The Discussion gives cocaine as implicated in 54 deaths and found in 105.
key_findings.note: Table 2 sums to 56 deaths with cocaine implicated (editors' calculation; reporting issue 6).

key_findings.finding: Ecstasy was implicated in 15 (2%) direct overdoses, 6 (1%) as the sole drug, and found post mortem in 20 (2.5%); it was implicated in 7 (23%) traumatic accidents, once as the sole drug.

Methadone was implicated in 101 (13%) direct overdoses, 4% as the sole drug, and found post mortem in 112 (14.0%); it was implicated in 19 (26%) drug-related medical-condition deaths. Other opiates (e.g., co-proxamol, dihydrocodeine) were implicated in 106 (13%) direct overdoses and 9 (23%) non-drug-related medical-condition deaths; amphetamines in 11 (1%) direct overdoses and 6 (15%) non-drug-related medical-condition deaths.
key_findings.note: Methadone in acute physical events is printed as 20 (19%) in Table 2 and as 19% in the text; 20 of 74 is 27% (reporting issue 4).

key_findings.finding: Counts of drug deaths differ by source, as the Introduction reports: coroners' verdicts of death from drug misuse rose 5% in 2000, from 573 to 605 (Allen, 2001); NP-SAD recorded 1,296 drug-related deaths in 2000; ONS reported 2,943 deaths in England and Wales in 1999 with drug poisoning as the underlying cause. The authors attribute the differences to differing data collection and recording.

The authors note that there was no standardized system of toxicological testing and reporting at inquest and no statutory requirement for coroners to give detailed information; NP-SAD returns rely on toxicology and death-certificate information; and because negative findings are not recorded, it is unclear whether substances not reported were absent or not tested for.

Heroin/morphine was implicated in over half of all the accidental deaths; of the direct overdose deaths, over half had heroin/morphine among the drugs implicated, and the Discussion says a third of 'those direct overdose cases' died after taking only heroin/morphine. No table gives sole-drug counts, and whether the third refers to all direct overdoses or to those with heroin/morphine is not clear.
key_findings.note: A third of all 802 direct overdoses would be about 267 deaths, a third of the 424 with heroin/morphine implicated about 141 (editors' calculation); neither can be checked against a table.

reporting_issues.issue: The case definition (accidental overdose under circumstances that did not suggest other causes of death; deaths deemed overdoses when nothing suggested otherwise) conflicts with the categorisation, which places 23% of the included deaths in other categories, including injuries and acute infections.
reporting_issues.consequence: What the 1,037 deaths have in common is unclear (apparently all accidental deaths reported to NP-SAD); the 23% cannot be read as overdoses that were misclassified. Because direct overdose was the default category when nothing in a coroner's return suggested otherwise (p. 68, 2.2), the 77% direct-overdose share is an upper limit and the 23% in other categories a lower limit, given the detail in the returns.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1's prevalence ratios are ratios of within-category percentages (women 20.3% against men 79.9% gives 0.3 for direct overdose), but the text reads them as risks. The women's direct-overdose ratio (0.3) carries the footnote for a 95% CI above 1.0. Printed ratios that do not match their own percentages (editors' calculations): in the no-fixed-abode row 0.8, 0.6, 0.6 and 0.4 are about ten times the ratios of the printed percentages (e.g., 6.7/85.9 = 0.08); the history-of-misuse ratio for drug-related medical conditions is printed 0.9 against 9.7/88.9 = 0.1, while the text gives 1.1; the employed ratio for traumatic accidents is printed 1.1 against 48.4/51.6 = 0.9.
reporting_issues.consequence: None of the risk statements by sex, age, employment, living arrangement or history of drug misuse can be cited; the table supports only descriptions of who died in each category.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results state that the 25–34 age group has the highest risk of death in all categories, but Table 1 gives a higher ratio for 35–44 than for 25–34 in non-drug-related medical conditions (15.0 against 12.0); the Discussion reads the same table as showing risk decreasing from age 25 for direct overdose, traumatic accidents, acute events and infections.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper's age statements contradict each other and its table; the age figures can be cited only as numbers of deaths.

reporting_issues.issue: Printed percentages that do not match their counts (editors' calculations): in Table 2, the acute physical event column (other opiates 7 printed as 5%, against 9%; methadone 20 as 19%, against 27%; anti-psychotics 4 as 4%, against 5%; alcohol 21 as 27%, against 28%) and cocaine in acute infections (2 printed as 1%, against 11%), while the text uses 19% for methadone in acute events; in Table 3, 9 of 40 printed as 22.0% (22.5%) and amphetamines 1 of 74 as 3.0% (1.4%); in Table 1, men and women add to 100.2% for direct overdose and 100.4% for acute events.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the counts, recomputing percentages; whether methadone was implicated in 20 or about 14 acute-event deaths cannot be settled from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: In several cells a drug is implicated in more deaths than it was found in post mortem: heroin/morphine in acute physical events (42 against 41), methadone in acute physical events (20 against 17), ecstasy in acute physical events (2 against 0), anti-psychotics in non-drug-related medical conditions (1 against 0), GHB (2 against 1) and anti-Parkinson drugs (3 against 2) in direct overdoses.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either drugs were named as implicated without being reported as found (possible when toxicology was not reported) or the tables contain transcription errors; the paper does not say which.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion gives cocaine as implicated in 54 deaths; the six category counts in Table 2 add up to more (editors' sum: 35 + 8 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 5 = 56).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the contrast with 105 deaths in which cocaine was found holds either way.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract calls the acute physical event category asphyxiation (7%), although it includes 22 aspiration pneumonias and 1 hypothermia, describes the data as from the United Kingdom although they cover England and Wales, and calls the design a retrospective cohort study; agreement was measured with phi rather than a chance-corrected statistic, and how disagreements between the two raters were resolved is not described.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the category as acute non-traumatic physical events (mostly aspiration), the setting as England and Wales, and the design as a cross-sectional series of deaths.
